questions.stem:
Statement: Hundreds of passengers were stranded at the railway station when a sudden technical failure cancelled all trains on the main line for over six hours.

Course of Action I: The railway authorities should arrange alternate bus transport for the stranded passengers immediately.
Course of Action II: The railway authorities should lodge an FIR against the technician responsible for the failure.

Which course(s) of action follow(s)?

options.option_text: Only Course I follows (immediate relief is necessary; FIR against a technician is premature without investigation)
Only Course II follows (punishing the responsible individual deters future failures)
Both Course I and Course II follow (both immediate relief and accountability are required)
Neither follows (technical failures are beyond administrative control)

questions.explanation: A is correct. Course I (arrange alternate transport) is a practical, immediate response to the problem — it directly addresses the hardship of stranded passengers. Course II (lodge FIR against a technician) is premature and punitive without establishing individual liability through investigation first. A technical failure can have many causes; blaming one technician without inquiry is not a sound course of action.

questions.stem:
Statement: A survey found that more than 40% of school children in a district are suffering from malnutrition due to poor mid-day meal quality.

Course of Action I: The district education authority should audit the mid-day meal suppliers and replace those providing substandard food.
Course of Action II: The government should immediately shut down all mid-day meal programmes across the district.

Which course(s) of action follow(s)?

options.option_text: Only Course I follows (audit and replace — targeted remediation; shutting the programme denies food to remaining 60%)
Only Course II follows (the programme has failed and must be suspended entirely)
Both Course I and Course II follow (both action and suspension are necessary)
Neither follows (malnutrition has many causes beyond mid-day meals)

questions.explanation: A is correct. Course I (audit and replace) is a targeted, constructive response — it fixes the quality problem without denying the benefit to children who are not yet malnourished. Course II (shut down the programme) is an extreme response that would harm the 60% of children who still benefit from the mid-day meal, and it does not address the root cause. Shutting a beneficial programme when reform is possible is not a sound course of action.

questions.stem:
Statement: A leading bank has reported a sharp increase in cases of online fraud involving the use of cloned debit cards targeting elderly customers.

Course of Action I: The bank should immediately issue chip-and-PIN cards to replace all magnetic stripe cards and educate customers on safe usage.
Course of Action II: The bank should advise all elderly customers to stop using debit cards and switch exclusively to cash transactions.

Which course(s) of action follow(s)?

options.option_text: Only Course I follows (technological upgrade is constructive; advising cash-only is regressive and impractical)
Only Course II follows (the simplest solution is to avoid digital transactions)
Both Course I and Course II follow (technological and behavioural change are both required)
Neither follows (fraud cannot be fully prevented by any action)

questions.explanation: A is correct. Course I (chip-and-PIN upgrade + education) directly addresses the cause — magnetic stripe cards are vulnerable to cloning, and chip cards are far more secure. This is a practical, effective, forward-looking response. Course II (advising cash-only) treats the symptom by avoidance rather than fixing the underlying security gap. It is also discriminatory and impractical for elderly customers in a digital-first environment.

questions.stem:
Statement: The city reported a 30% increase in road accidents at a particular intersection over the past year.

Course of Action I: The traffic police should deploy an officer at that intersection during peak hours.
Course of Action II: The municipal corporation should study the intersection's design and install proper signage and signals.

Which course(s) of action follow(s)?

options.option_text: Only Course I follows (deploying police is immediate and effective)
Only Course II follows (engineering improvement is more sustainable)
Both Course I and Course II follow (short-term police presence and long-term design improvements are both needed)
Neither follows (accidents cannot be prevented at a particular intersection)

questions.explanation: C is correct. Both courses are valid and complementary. Course I (deploy officer during peak hours) provides an immediate, temporary solution to manage traffic flow and reduce accidents now. Course II (study design and install signals) is the long-term structural remedy — it addresses the root cause of the accidents through engineering improvements. Together, they constitute a complete response to the problem.

questions.stem:
Statement: A large number of residents in an urban locality are dumping solid waste in the open near a residential area, creating serious hygiene problems.

Course of Action I: The local authorities should provide proper dustbins at regular intervals and increase the frequency of garbage collection.
Course of Action II: The local authorities should impose heavy fines on those found dumping waste openly.

Which course(s) of action follow(s)?

options.option_text: Only Course I follows (providing infrastructure is more effective than punitive measures alone)
Only Course II follows (fines create deterrence and stop the behaviour immediately)
Both Course I and Course II follow (both infrastructure provision and deterrence are required)
Neither follows (open dumping is a cultural problem that policy cannot solve quickly)

questions.explanation: C is correct. Both courses are sound. Course I addresses the reason residents dump waste openly — a lack of accessible infrastructure. Without dustbins, even willing residents have no alternative. Course II creates a deterrent that discourages those who would dump even with infrastructure available. Together, they cover both the supply-side gap (no bins) and the compliance gap (no consequence). Either alone is incomplete.

questions.stem:
Statement: A study revealed that a significant number of students in rural government schools drop out before completing Class 8 because their families need them to work to supplement household income.

Course of Action I: The government should make attendance at school mandatory under strict legal penalty for all students up to Class 8.
Course of Action II: The government should introduce conditional cash transfers to poor families, providing financial support contingent on children's regular school attendance.

Which course(s) of action follow(s)?

options.option_text: Only Course I follows (mandatory attendance ensures children stay in school)
Only Course II follows (addressing economic compulsion is more humane and effective than penalties)
Both Course I and Course II follow (legal mandate and incentives both drive attendance)
Neither follows (economic compulsion cannot be addressed through school policy)

questions.explanation: B is correct. The statement identifies ECONOMIC COMPULSION as the root cause of dropout — families need the child's labour income. Course I (legal penalty for non-attendance) does not address this root cause; penalising already-poor families for economic compulsion is counterproductive and harmful. Course II (conditional cash transfer) directly addresses the economic gap — compensating families financially for keeping children in school has been proven effective (MGNREGA, Kanya Sumangala, PAHAL schemes). I alone is harsh without addressing root cause; both together would not make sense as the penalty in I conflicts with the supportive approach in II.

questions.stem:
Statement: Reports indicate that a number of patients are being overcharged at private hospitals in a city, and many complaints go unresolved for months.

Course of Action I: The state government should set up a dedicated healthcare grievance redressal authority with powers to act within 30 days.
Course of Action II: The government should nationalise all private hospitals to prevent overcharging.

Which course(s) of action follow(s)?

options.option_text: Only Course I follows (a targeted grievance authority is proportionate; nationalisation is extreme)
Only Course II follows (nationalisation permanently eliminates the profit motive behind overcharging)
Both Course I and Course II follow (regulation and ownership change are both needed)
Neither follows (private hospitals cannot be regulated effectively)

questions.explanation: A is correct. Course I (grievance authority with time-bound powers) is a proportionate, actionable policy response that addresses the complaint resolution gap. Course II (nationalise all private hospitals) is an extreme, sweeping action disproportionate to the problem. Nationalisation would have massive fiscal and operational consequences and is not a standard course of action for the stated problem. The rule of thumb: radical structural solutions (nationalise, shut down) are rarely the correct course of action in these questions unless the problem is catastrophic with no alternative.

questions.stem:
Statement: In a coastal city, a rising sea level has caused saltwater intrusion into freshwater sources, affecting the drinking water supply of over two lakh residents.

Course of Action I: The city municipal corporation should immediately set up water purification plants and distribute packaged drinking water to affected residents.
Course of Action II: The municipal corporation should relocate all two lakh residents to inland areas within one month.

Which course(s) of action follow(s)?

options.option_text: Only Course I follows (water provision is immediate and feasible; mass relocation in a month is impractical)
Only Course II follows (relocation prevents future exposure to sea-level-related problems)
Both Course I and Course II follow (immediate water supply and long-term relocation both make sense)
Neither follows (climate change effects cannot be managed by local bodies)

questions.explanation: A is correct. Course I (purification plants + packaged water) is a practical, immediate solution to the drinking water crisis. It is feasible and directly addresses the stated problem. Course II (relocate two lakh residents in one month) is physically and logistically impossible in that timeframe — and mass relocation raises far broader social, legal, and financial issues that go beyond the scope of a municipal response to a water problem. The timeframe '1 month' makes Course II unrealistic.

questions.stem:
Statement: A college has reported that a large number of students are accessing gaming websites during class hours using the institution's Wi-Fi, leading to poor academic outcomes.

Course of Action I: The college should install content filtering software to block gaming websites on the institutional network during class hours.
Course of Action II: The college should permanently ban all students found accessing gaming websites from attending any further classes.

Which course(s) of action follow(s)?

options.option_text: Only Course I follows (technical filtering is proportionate; permanent banning for browsing is extreme)
Only Course II follows (strong punishment creates effective deterrence)
Both Course I and Course II follow (both filtering and strict penalties are required)
Neither follows (students' internet usage is a personal matter)

questions.explanation: A is correct. Course I (content filtering) is a proportionate technical solution that directly prevents gaming during class hours without punishing any individual. Course II (permanent ban from classes) is a grossly disproportionate punishment for the stated problem — gaming on campus Wi-Fi during class does not warrant expulsion from all future classes. Courses of action that are extreme or disproportionate to the problem are not considered sound responses in logical reasoning questions.

questions.stem:
Statement: Data shows that the accident rate on a particular state highway rises sharply during foggy winter nights, with most accidents involving heavy trucks.

Course of Action I: The state transport department should issue an advisory recommending that truck drivers use fog lights and reduce speed during foggy conditions on that highway.
Course of Action II: The state should completely ban all truck movement on that highway between November and February.

Which course(s) of action follow(s)?

options.option_text: Only Course I follows (advisory is practical; seasonal highway ban disrupts essential supply chains disproportionately)
Only Course II follows (a seasonal ban completely eliminates the identified risk)
Both Course I and Course II follow (advisory plus ban gives maximum safety)
Neither follows (fog-related accidents on highways cannot be prevented by policy)

questions.explanation: A is correct. Course I (advisory on fog lights and reduced speed) directly addresses the behaviour contributing to accidents — it provides actionable guidance to drivers and is proportionate to the problem. Course II (complete truck ban for 4 months) is a disproportionate response — trucks carry essential goods, and a 4-month ban would massively disrupt supply chains. More targeted measures (speed limits, mandatory fog lights, patrol increases) are the appropriate response. Extreme blanket bans are rarely the correct course of action.
